West Virginia's high electricity costs are driven by a combination of historical dependence on coal and modern infrastructure pressures. While the state once enjoyed some of the lowest rates in the country, prices have surged rising nearly 34% between 2019 and 2024 largely because the state generates about 86% of its power from aging coal plants that are increasingly expensive to maintain and struggle to compete with cheaper natural gas and renewables.  

Beyond fuel costs, residential bills are further strained by a massive "data center boom" in the region, which has forced the regional grid operator (PJM) to invest billions in new transmission lines. 

West Virginia ratepayers are expected to contribute over $440 million for projects primarily serving these out of state facilities. Compounding these factors are a shrinking state population and the high cost of upgrading a "decrepit" grid against extreme weather, creating a significant energy burden for residents whose median incomes have not kept pace with these soaring utility expenses.

Fighting high electricity costs in West Virginia requires a mix of immediate personal action and long term community advocacy. — INVER GROVE HEIGHTS APPROVES PAUSE ON DATA CENTERS AS AI BOOM SPARKS CONCERNS 

Inver Grove Heights has officially hit pause on proposed data center developments as concerns continue growing across Minnesota over the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure.

In a split 3-2 vote this week, the Inver Grove Heights City Council approved a one-year moratorium on new data centers while city officials study the possible long-term impacts these facilities could have on the community.

The debate centered around a proposed data center project planned for the former Travel Tags site on Carmen Avenue.

The developer behind the proposal — California-based Fortress Investment Group — argued the project would not resemble the massive “mega data centers” being built elsewhere in Minnesota and claimed its water usage would be comparable to only a few homes.

Despite those assurances, concerns remained over future environmental impacts, power usage, infrastructure strain, and how quickly data centers tied to the AI industry are spreading throughout the state.

Residents also voiced frustration after the council vote because public comment was not allowed before the moratorium was approved. Council members said they believed they had already received enough community input on the issue.

Inver Grove Heights now joins Eagan and other Minnesota communities attempting to get ahead of the growing demand for data centers fueled by artificial intelligence and cloud computing exp

bill_title: Data centers; noise abatement.
post_text:
⚡️🔌 Data centers use a staggering amount of electricity. As of 2022, they consumed about 21% of Virginia’s power, but they are the only growing sector of electricity demand in the state. In fact, there are so many new facilities being proposed and approved that this single industry is projected to drive Virginia's peak energy demand to double from current levels by 2040.

This explosive growth threatens to derail state efforts to meet climate goals, improve air and water quality, advance land conservation, and protect national and state parks. 

To make matters even worse, ordinary ratepayers throughout the state will foot the bill to build out the electric transmission and generation projects that are required to keep the data center industry afloat. Yet, the Commonwealth does not currently have any regulatory oversight of data center development. 

Learn more and take action at https://pecva.org/datacenters

Watch the full video at https://youtu.be/fAPusgiz4B8?si=GmMAh4iNGPewchqO
